patterns.name: Pronoun case
patterns.summary: Subject, object, and possessive forms: io / me / mi.
patterns.description: Interlingua keeps the case system Latin had on pronouns, even though it drops it everywhere else. Each person has a subject form (io, tu, ille, illa, nos, vos, illes), an object form (me, te, le, la, nos, vos, les), a possessive adjective (mi, tu, su, nostre, lor), and a possessive pronoun (mie, tue, sue, nostre, lore). Every Romance language makes the same distinctions with recognisably related forms, so this table is the highest-value thing to memorise here: it unlocks the pronoun systems of four languages at once.
patterns.source_note: Gode & Blair, Interlingua: A Grammar of the International Language, 2nd ed. 1955, §54 (p. 21)

examples.note: Subject form: io.
Object form: me, not io.
nos serves as both subject and object; les is the plural object form.
The possessive pronoun mie, distinct from the adjective mi, and normally with the article.
su covers his, her, and its, and never agrees with what is owned. Spanish su behaves the same way; French and Italian do not, and pick the form from the thing owned.

parallels.it: Sua sorella ama il suo cane.
parallels.pt: A irmã dele ama o cão dele.

patterns.name: Object pronouns before the verb
patterns.summary: Io le vide, not *Io vide le — the object pronoun comes first.
patterns.description: An unstressed object pronoun goes in front of a finite verb: 'Io le vide', literally 'I him see'. English puts it after, so this needs unlearning rather than learning, and it is one of the first things that makes a beginner's Spanish or French sound wrong. Every Romance language does the same. The exception is worth as much as the rule: after an infinitive, a participle, or an imperative the pronoun follows instead, giving 'Io vole vider le'. Spanish and Portuguese agree ('quiero verlo'), Italian agrees ('voglio vederlo'), and French does not, keeping the pronoun before the infinitive ('je veux le voir').
patterns.source_note: Gode & Blair, Interlingua: A Grammar of the International Language, 2nd ed. 1955, §§67–69 (p. 25)

examples.note: Object before the finite verb.
With both a negator and a pronoun, the pronoun sits closer to the verb: non lo sape.
After an infinitive the pronoun follows. French is the outlier and keeps it in front: je veux le voir.
After an imperative the pronoun follows, as it does across Romance.
Reflexive se follows the same placement rule. Romance uses reflexives far more widely than English does, often where English would use a passive.

patterns.name: The three infinitive classes
patterns.summary: -ar, -er, -ir: the class predicts the target-language infinitive.
patterns.description: Interlingua verbs end in -ar, -er, or -ir, the same three classes Latin left to every Romance language. The class is worth knowing because it predicts the shape of the infinitive in the target: Italian adds a vowel (cantar to cantare), Spanish and Portuguese usually leave -ar and -ir alone, and French reshapes -ar to -er (cantar to chanter). It also predicts which conjugation the verb will take once you get to a language that conjugates.
patterns.source_note: Gode & Blair, Interlingua: A Grammar of the International Language, 2nd ed. 1955, §§80ff (pp. 29ff)

examples.note: First class. Regular across all four targets.
Second class. French contracts to -re.
Third class. Unchanged in three of the four targets.
Second class, and a reminder that the class predicts the ending, not the stem: every target reshapes scrib- differently.

patterns.name: Where the scaffold stops: verb agreement
patterns.summary: Interlingua does not conjugate. Every target language does.
patterns.description: Interlingua uses one verb form for every person: io canta, tu canta, ille canta, nos canta. This is the largest single simplification in the language, and the one place where relying on Interlingua will actively mislead you, because all four target languages inflect the verb for person and number and none of them treat it as optional. The pattern is drilled the other way round from the others: the Interlingua sentence is the prompt, and the point is to notice how much the target adds. Use Interlingua for the vocabulary and the word order, and expect to learn conjugation from scratch.
patterns.source_note: Gode & Blair, Interlingua: A Grammar of the International Language, 2nd ed. 1955, §§80ff (pp. 29ff)

examples.note: Same verb form as io canta. No target language agrees.
Still canta. Compare how far the four targets diverge here.
One past tense, -va, where Romance distinguishes preterite from imperfect. Spanish cantaron and cantaban are both cantava in Interlingua.

patterns.name: Building words from affixes
patterns.summary: One root plus a productive affix: nation, national, nationalitate.
patterns.description: Interlingua is built to be extended by analogy. A root takes a productive affix and the result is a real word, so nation gives national, nationalitate, nationalismo, nationalista, and international, all without consulting a dictionary. The affixes are the ones Romance already shares, which is what makes this the highest-leverage pattern in the language: learning that -itate marks a quality gets you Spanish -idad, French -ité, Italian -ità, and Portuguese -idade in one step, and those endings are stable enough to guess through.
patterns.source_note: Gode & Blair, Interlingua: A Grammar of the International Language, 2nd ed. 1955, §§135ff (pp. 56ff)

examples.prompt: Which suffix turns an adjective into the quality it names?
examples.note: -itate names a quality. Compare Spanish -idad, French -ité.

examples.prompt: Which suffix makes an adverb from an adjective?
examples.note: -mente attaches to the full adjective. Three of the four targets use the same suffix; French wore it down to -ment.
-abile from -ar verbs, -ibile from -er and -ir verbs.

examples.prompt: Which suffix names the shop or premises dealing in something?
examples.note: Paired with -ero for the person: lactero, a milkman.
Surfaces as des- in Spanish and Portuguese, dé- in French.

examples.prompt: Which suffix names the practitioner of an art or science?
examples.note: Freely productive: any field name takes it, so saxophone gives saxophonista.
